1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Brings the second knight to its natural square, adds control of d5 and e4 and prepares the e4 break. White commits to nothing else yet: a pin, an exchange on d5 or quiet development all remain open, and Black has to be ready for each of them.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5.strategy: Pins the f6-knight to the queen, tying down one of the defenders of d5 and making Black's freeing plans harder. Black will want to break the pin and get the king safe; White hopes to keep a space edge and a long manoeuvring game.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Traditional Variation

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop towards d5 and the queenside, trading a quick centre for lasting long-diagonal pressure. White's c4 pawn can be left loose, because opening the diagonal is worth more; Black gets a solid centre but must live with the bishop for the whole game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3.strategy: Quiet and solid: it guards d4 and opens the f1-bishop, but it shuts the c1-bishop in behind its own pawns, the same problem Black has on the other wing. White gives up both the pin and the long-diagonal pressure, so the game becomes slow and Black equalises easily.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7.strategy: The classical set-up: the bishop clears the way for castling and keeps the pawn chain intact. Black stays solid and waits, the c8-bishop remaining the long-term task; White has the freer development and a small space edge to play with.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, before White has castled, aiming for free piece play. The cost is a structure in which Black often ends up with an isolated or hanging central pawn pair that White can target, so the dynamic activity has to make up for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c6.strategy: Backs d5 with the c-pawn and builds a very solid chain, giving up the ...c5 break. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind e6 for now; Black keeps the option of taking on c4 and holding the pawn, which leads to sharp, double-edged play.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6.strategy: Prepares to free the light-squared bishop on the long diagonal without a pawn break. It is slower than the main set-ups: d5 gets less support, and after the exchange on d5 a check on b5 has to be answered with care.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Be7.strategy: Prepares castling and leaves the choice open: Black can take on c4 later or keep the centre closed. It is the flexible way to develop while White decides how to handle the bishop and the c4 pawn, and the dark-squared bishop stays out of harm.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6.strategy: Shields d5 with a pawn against the long diagonal, so the g2-bishop meets a wall. Black accepts a compact but cramped position with the c8-bishop shut in behind e6, in return for a solid centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bb4+.strategy: Checks to force a concession in White's set-up: the c1-bishop, usually, has to take an awkward square on d2. The cost is that the bishop may have to be traded or retreat later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the g5-bishop at once: retreat and keep the pin, or exchange for the knight. With White's queen's knight still at home, the immediate exchange on f6 puts no pressure on d5, so Black can ask the question safely.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 h6.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4+.strategy: Counters the pin with a pin of its own: the check forces a block, and a knight arriving on c3 stands pinned to the king, so White cannot simply carry on with its centre plans. The game becomes sharper and more double-edged.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4+.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Vienna Variation

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with the c-pawn, so the f6-knight is no longer essential to its defence and the pin loses much of its sting. Black accepts a cramped position with the c8-bishop shut in behind e6, in return for a very solid centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and gives up the centre without getting a concession first. Black cannot expect to keep the pawn: White regains it in its own time with a developing move and builds a strong centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nbd.strategy: Develops the queen's knight to guard c4, so ...dxc4 would win no pawn, and keeps the e-pawn free for a solid centre. White keeps the bishop on g5 bearing down on f6; the price is that the knight on d2 can be pinned against the king by ...Qa5.

Adds a second defender to f6, so the pin by the bishop on g5 costs Black nothing, and supports a later central break with ...e5. Black settles for a compact c6-d5-e6 pawn chain, at the price of a light-squared bishop that stays shut in behind e6.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nbd.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Capablanca Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 c6 5.Nbd.strategy: Backs up d4 with a second guard, frees the king's bishop and prepares castling, while the knight on d2 holds c4. A patient, solid set-up: White keeps the bishop on g5 pinning down f6 and aims for a slow build-up in the centre rather than quick tactics.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.Q.strategy: Wins the c4 pawn back with check: Black cannot hold it by force, so White spends no tempo regaining it and keeps the bishop on g5 bearing on the f6 knight. Black has to find the least awkward way to block the check, and White's queen reaches an active square.

Blocks the check with a pawn, so no piece is misplaced, and prepares ...b5 to chase the queen once it recaptures on c4. Black accepts that the extra pawn is gone and aims for a solid queenside and quick development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.Q.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Traditional Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5 dxc4 5.Q.strategy: Recaptures and puts the queen on an active diagonal, eyeing the e6 pawn, with White ahead in development. The queen is exposed to a pawn push on the queenside, so it will need a good square soon, but the Queen's Gambit pawn is regained at once.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and attacks d5 a second time, so Black will want the fianchettoed bishop as a further defender of the pawn there. White keeps the choice between exchanging in the centre and a quiet build-up with the king's bishop and castling.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.b3.strategy: Meets the fianchetto with a fianchetto of its own: the bishop on b2 will back the d4 pawn and look at the centre. The set-up is solid and flexible but quiet, with less pressure on d5 than the knight move brings; neither side has a clear edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Fianchettoes the bishop to the long diagonal, where it defends d5 and stands ready for when the centre opens. For now it looks at its own pawn, so it comes alive only after a central pawn break; in return Black gets a solid, flexible set-up that holds the centre without committing the king's bishop.

Places the bishop on the b8-h2 diagonal aiming at the kingside, but it is exposed on d6. Once the centre is opened, White can gain time by attacking it with a knight, so Black loses time while White develops.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.b3 B.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up: both queen's bishops head for the long diagonal behind their d-pawns, so the game becomes a fight over the first pawn break in the centre.
Develops the king's bishop on the diagonal aimed at h7 and backs a later e4 advance. It prepares castling and keeps all of White's central plans open, while the pawns on b3 and e3 make a solid base.
Completes queenside development and supports the f6 knight and the e5 square. It prepares a pawn break in the centre, at the price of a slightly cramped queenside.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops the bishop to its best diagonal, where it eyes h7, and prepares castling, keeping the capture on d5 in reserve. White stays flexible and can choose its central plan after Black has shown the set-up, while the d6 bishop gets in the way of Black's own pieces.

Settles the tension in the centre. After the recapture with the e-pawn the symmetrical structure leaves the bishop on d6 exposed to a knight jump to b5, which wins White a tempo, while White's pieces are ready to develop freely.
Castles at once. The knight on f6 guards h7 against the bishop on d3, so the king is safe. Black keeps the central tension and chooses between a pawn break in the centre and capturing on c4 later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Exchange Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 b6 5.Nc3.strategy: Recaptures towards the centre. The e6 pawn, which blocked the light-squared bishop, leaves, and the bishop gets its diagonal; the price is that the bishop on d6 can be attacked by a knight jump to b5, so Black has to be ready to lose a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.Nc3.strategy: Brings out the knight and adds pressure on d5 and e4, reaching the classical set-up of this opening. White keeps every plan open, and the real contest is whether Black can free the light-squared bishop that the e6 pawn locks in.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.b3.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, where it supports the d4 pawn and eyes the centre. The b3 pawn also firms up c4, so taking on c4 would only help White build a broad centre. A restrained plan, with less immediate pressure on d5 than the knight move.

Castles and completes the kingside. Black has no reason to hurry against a slow set-up: the usual plan is the pawn break against White's centre, which Black prepares by finishing development first and keeping the d5 pawn firm.

Puts the bishop on its long diagonal at once and keeps the king's bishop flexible. It supports the d4 pawn and eyes the centre; White keeps the choice of where the other bishop goes, and the game becomes a quiet fight for space in the centre.

Develops the king's bishop on the diagonal aimed at h7 and prepares to castle. The bishop is now committed, which gives Black the chance to release the tension in the centre or to fianchetto the light-squared bishop and free it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.b3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Be7 5.b3.strategy: Solves the problem of the light-squared bishop by fianchettoing it, where it can look along the long diagonal once the centre opens. Black commits to fighting for the centre with a pawn break or with captures on c4, not to a slow pawn chain on c6.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 c5 5.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn before Black can build a full centre, forcing Black to decide the pawn structure. The tension between the c5 and d4 pawns then decides the game, and either side can end up with an isolated pawn and active pieces as compensation.

Recaptures with the e-pawn, keeping the knight on f6 and opening the diagonal of the light-squared bishop. Black gets a duo of pawns on c5 and d5 against the d4 pawn. If White later takes on c5, Black has an isolated d-pawn but active piece play.

Develops the knight with pressure on d5 and gives the knight possible jumps to b5 and d5. White's pieces aim at Black's central pawns, which must be defended, and the game turns on whether Black's active pieces compensate for the structure.
Takes the b5 square away from White's bishop and knight, but spends a tempo on a flank move while White's pieces take over the centre and the pawns on c5 and d5 are left to be challenged.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bb4+ 5.Bd.strategy: Meets the check by developing the queen's bishop and offering the trade, keeping the fianchetto plan. The bishop is not best placed on d2, but Black's bishop must now decide whether to retreat or to exchange, so the check costs Black time.

Retreats instead of exchanging, keeping the bishop pair at the cost of a tempo. White's bishop is not on the best square on d2, so the tempo is not a high price. A solid choice that keeps the position closed and Black's structure healthy.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop sits behind the f3 knight, looking at the long diagonal, and the king gets a safe home after castling. White plans long-term queenside and centre pressure while Black holds a solid structure.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Be7 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop on the long diagonal presses on d5 and the queenside, a pressure that grows once the f3-knight moves. White trades a quick central grab for lasting pressure, with the king a move from castling.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop, the move behind the whole set-up. Black's c6 and d5 pawns shield the long diagonal for now, so White's pressure is slow and positional: build behind the pawns, keep the king safe, and wait for the centre to open.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.name: Catalan Opening: Open Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 c6 5.Bg2.strategy: Takes the pawn and tries to keep it with ...b5, which the c6 pawn supports. The capture also opens the long diagonal in front of White's bishop. If White regains the pawn, Black has at least gained time; if not, Black must hold the weakened queenside.
